claim: Ferroptosis is a distinct iron-dependent programmed cell death.
source: Ferroptosis is a distinct iron-dependent programmed cell death and plays important roles in tumor suppression.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about ferroptosis that is supported by established scientific knowledge and is cited in the introduction with reference to Dixon et al., 2012.

claim: Ferroptosis plays important roles in tumor suppression.
source: Ferroptosis is a distinct iron-dependent programmed cell death and plays important roles in tumor suppression.
evidence: This statement is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations in the introduction.

claim: RUNX2 has two types of transcripts produced by two alternative promoters.
source: RUNX2 has two types of transcripts produced by two alternative promoters.
evidence: This is supported by the schematic diagram in Figure 1A showing the two promoters (P1 and P2) and the resulting isoforms.

claim: RUNX2 isoform II is a novel ferroptosis and apoptosis suppressor.
source: In the present study, we surprisingly find that RUNX2 isoform II is a novel ferroptosis and apoptosis suppressor.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experimental data including ROS levels, lipid peroxidation, and apoptosis assays shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: RUNX2 isoform II can bind to the promoter of peroxiredoxin-2 (PRDX2).
source: RUNX2 isoform II can bind to the promoter of peroxiredoxin-2 (PRDX2), a ferroptosis inhibitor, and activate its expression.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4H and 4I demonstrating direct binding of RUNX2 isoform II to the PRDX2 promoter.

claim: RUNX2 isoform II activates PRDX2 expression.
source: RUNX2 isoform II can bind to the promoter of peroxiredoxin-2 (PRDX2), a ferroptosis inhibitor, and activate its expression.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and western blot data in Figure 4B, 4C, 4E, and 4F showing that isoform II knockdown decreases PRDX2 expression and overexpression increases it.

claim: Knockdown of RUNX2 isoform II suppresses cell proliferation in vitro in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).
source: Knockdown of RUNX2 isoform II suppresses cell proliferation in vitro and tumorigenesis in vivo in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting and colony formation assays shown in Figure 2C, 2D, and 2E.

claim: Knockdown of RUNX2 isoform II suppresses tumorigenesis in vivo in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).
source: Knockdown of RUNX2 isoform II suppresses cell proliferation in vitro and tumorigenesis in vivo in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC).
evidence: This is supported by nude mice xenograft experiments shown in Figure 2G-J demonstrating reduced tumor growth and weight.

claim: Homeobox A10 (HOXA10) is an upstream positive regulator of RUNX2 isoform II.
source: Interestingly, homeobox A10 (HOXA10), an upstream positive regulator of RUNX2 isoform II, is required for the inhibition of ferroptosis and apoptosis through the RUNX2 isoform II/PRDX2 pathway.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5A showing that HOXA10 knockdown reduces isoform II expression.

claim: HOXA10 is required for the inhibition of ferroptosis through the RUNX2 isoform II/PRDX2 pathway.
source: Interestingly, homeobox A10 (HOXA10), an upstream positive regulator of RUNX2 isoform II, is required for the inhibition of ferroptosis and apoptosis through the RUNX2 isoform II/PRDX2 pathway.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 6 and 7 showing that HOXA10 knockdown increases ROS and lipid peroxidation, and that these effects can be rescued by isoform II or PRDX2 overexpression.

claim: HOXA10 is required for the inhibition of apoptosis through the RUNX2 isoform II/PRDX2 pathway.
source: Interestingly, homeobox A10 (HOXA10), an upstream positive regulator of RUNX2 isoform II, is required for the inhibition of ferroptosis and apoptosis through the RUNX2 isoform II/PRDX2 pathway.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 5D, 6F, and 7B showing that HOXA10 knockdown increases apoptosis, and that this effect can be rescued by isoform II overexpression.

claim: RUNX2 isoform II is overexpressed in OSCC.
source: Consistently, RUNX2 isoform II is overexpressed in OSCC, and associated with OSCC progression and poor prognosis.
evidence: This is supported by TCGA data analysis in Figure 1C showing significantly higher PSI values of exon 1.1 (isoform II) in OSCC patients compared to normal controls, and by RT-PCR data from clinical samples in Figure 1G-I.

claim: RUNX2 isoform II is associated with OSCC progression.
source: Consistently, RUNX2 isoform II is overexpressed in OSCC, and associated with OSCC progression and poor prognosis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1E showing that patients with clinical stage IV have higher levels of isoform II compared to those with stage I, II, and III.

claim: RUNX2 isoform II is associated with poor prognosis in OSCC.
source: Consistently, RUNX2 isoform II is overexpressed in OSCC, and associated with OSCC progression and poor prognosis.
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis in Figure 1F showing that patients with higher isoform II expression have significantly shorter overall survival.

claim: Ferroptosis is characterized by the accumulation of lipid peroxidation and the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Ferroptosis, a form of non-apoptotic programmed cell death, is an iron-dependent death and is characterized by the accumulation of lipid peroxidation and the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Dixon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by established scientific knowledge and citation to Dixon et al., 2012.

claim: Targeting ferroptosis might provide new therapeutic opportunities in treating cancers.
source: Ferroptosis has sparked great interest as targeting ferroptosis might provide new therapeutic opportunities in treating cancers.
evidence: This is a statement based on inference from the emerging evidence about ferroptosis in cancer treatment.

claim: Ferroptosis may function as a potent tumor suppressor in the progression of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC).
source: Emerging evidence indicates that ferroptosis may function as a potent tumor suppressor in the progression of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) (Li et al., 2022b; Lu et al., 2022), including oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) (Sun et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to recent literature (Li et al., 2022b; Lu et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2021).

claim: Triggering ferroptosis can overcome OSCC-acquired drug resistance such as cisplatin-induced resistance.
source: Furthermore, triggering ferroptosis can overcome OSCC-acquired drug resistance such as cisplatin-induced resistance (Han et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Han et al., 2022.

claim: The induction of ferroptosis is an attractive strategy for OSCC therapy.
source: Therefore, the induction of ferroptosis is an attractive strategy for OSCC therapy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the previous statements about ferroptosis in OSCC.

claim: The extrinsic pathways of ferroptosis are initiated by the inhibition of cell membrane transporters such as the cystine/glutamate transporter system xc-.
source: The extrinsic pathways are initiated by the inhibition of cell membrane transporters such as the cystine/glutamate transporter system xc- or by the activation of the iron transporters transferrin (TF) and lactotransferrin (LTF).
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanisms of ferroptosis based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The extrinsic pathways of ferroptosis are initiated by the activation of the iron transporters transferrin (TF) and lactotransferrin (LTF).
source: The extrinsic pathways are initiated by the inhibition of cell membrane transporters such as the cystine/glutamate transporter system xc- or by the activation of the iron transporters transferrin (TF) and lactotransferrin (LTF).
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanisms of ferroptosis based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The intrinsic pathway of ferroptosis is activated by the blockade of intracellular antioxidant enzymes like glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4).
source: The intrinsic pathway is activated by the blockade of intracellular antioxidant enzymes like glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4).
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanisms of ferroptosis based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: RUNX2 is critical for osteogenesis.
source: The RUNT-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2), a member of the RUNT-related transcription factor family, is critical for osteogenesis (Bruderer et al., 2014) and has been extensively studied in the development of bone and tooth (Wen et al., 2020; Ziros et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Bruderer et al., 2014; Wen et al., 2020; Ziros et al., 2008.

claim: RUNX2 promotes cancer metastasis and invasion in a variety of cancers, including breast cancer.
source: Previous studies revealed that RUNX2 promotes cancer metastasis and invasion in a variety of cancers, including breast cancer (Chang et al., 2014), thyroid cancer (Sancisi et al., 2012), colorectal cancer (Ji et al., 2019), prostate cancer (Akech et al., 2010), lung cancer (Herreño et al., 2019), and HNSCC (Chang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: RUNX2 promotes cancer metastasis and invasion in thyroid cancer.
source: Previous studies revealed that RUNX2 promotes cancer metastasis and invasion in a variety of cancers, including breast cancer (Chang et al., 2014), thyroid cancer (Sancisi et al., 2012), colorectal cancer (Ji et al., 2019), prostate cancer (Akech et al., 2010), lung cancer (Herreño et al., 2019), and HNSCC (Chang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sancisi et al., 2012.

claim: RUNX2 promotes cancer metastasis and invasion in colorectal cancer.
source: Previous studies revealed that RUNX2 promotes cancer metastasis and invasion in a variety of cancers, including breast cancer (Chang et al., 2014), thyroid cancer (Sancisi et al., 2012), colorectal cancer (Ji et al., 2019), prostate cancer (Akech et al., 2010), lung cancer (Herreño et al., 2019), and HNSCC (Chang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Ji et al., 2019.

claim: RUNX2 promotes cancer metastasis and invasion in prostate cancer.
source: Previous studies revealed that RUNX2 promotes cancer metastasis and invasion in a variety of cancers, including breast cancer (Chang et al., 2014), thyroid cancer (Sancisi et al., 2012), colorectal cancer (Ji et al., 2019), prostate cancer (Akech et al., 2010), lung cancer (Herreño et al., 2019), and HNSCC (Chang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Akech et al., 2010.

claim: RUNX2 promotes cancer metastasis and invasion in lung cancer.
source: Previous studies revealed that RUNX2 promotes cancer metastasis and invasion in a variety of cancers, including breast cancer (Chang et al., 2014), thyroid cancer (Sancisi et al., 2012), colorectal cancer (Ji et al., 2019), prostate cancer (Akech et al., 2010), lung cancer (Herreño et al., 2019), and HNSCC (Chang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Herreño et al., 2019.

claim: RUNX2 promotes cancer metastasis and invasion in HNSCC.
source: Previous studies revealed that RUNX2 promotes cancer metastasis and invasion in a variety of cancers, including breast cancer (Chang et al., 2014), thyroid cancer (Sancisi et al., 2012), colorectal cancer (Ji et al., 2019), prostate cancer (Akech et al., 2010), lung cancer (Herreño et al., 2019), and HNSCC (Chang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Chang et al., 2016.

claim: RUNX2 gene is composed of two promoters that generate two types of isoforms, isoform II derived from promoter 1 (P1) and isoform I from promoter 2 (P2).
source: RUNX2 gene is composed of two promoters that in turn generate two types of isoforms, isoform II derived from promoter 1 (P1) and isoform I from promoter 2 (P2).
evidence: This is supported by the schematic diagram in Figure 1A and is established knowledge about RUNX2 gene structure.

claim: RUNX2 isoforms contain distinct N-terminal sequences.
source: These isoforms contain distinct N-terminal sequences.
evidence: This is a statement about the structural differences between RUNX2 isoforms based on established knowledge.

claim: OSCC is one of the most common malignant cancers in the world, especially in areas with low Human Development Index.
source: OSCC is one of the most common malignant cancers in the world, especially in areas with low Human Development Index (Sung et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sung et al., 2021.

claim: The treatment of OSCC has progressed over time from surgery alone to comprehensive series of therapies, including radiation, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy.
source: The treatment of OSCC has progressed over time from surgery alone to comprehensive series of therapies, including radiation, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy (Chi et al., 2015; Kang et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Chi et al., 2015; Kang et al., 2015.

claim: The 5-year overall survival rate of OSCC is around 50–60%.
source: Despite a lot of advances in treatment modalities, the 5-year overall survival rate is around 50–60% (Jäwert et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Jäwert et al., 2021.

claim: The expression levels of total RUNX2 were slightly higher in TCGA OSCC tissues than those in normal controls, but there was no statistically significant difference.
source: The expression levels of total RUNX2 were slightly higher in TCGA OSCC tissues than those in normal controls, but there was no statistically significant difference (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The expression levels of isoform II (indicated by PSI, percent-splice-in, the usage of exon 1.1 in total RUNX2 transcripts) in OSCC patients were 1.46-fold significantly higher than those in normal controls.
source: The expression levels of isoform II (indicated by PSI, percent-splice-in, the usage of exon 1.1 in total RUNX2 transcripts) in OSCC patients were 1.46-fold significantly higher than those in normal controls (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The expression levels of isoform I were lower in OSCC patients than those in normal controls.
source: In contrast, the expression levels of isoform I were lower than those in normal controls (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Patients with clinical stage I, II, and III showed lower levels of isoform II compared with those with stage IV.
source: Moreover, patients with clinical stage I, II, and III showed lower levels of isoform II compared with those with stage IV (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Patients with higher isoform II showed significantly shorter overall survival.
source: Patients with higher isoform II showed significantly shorter overall survival (Figure 1F), whereas patients with higher isoform I showed longer overall survival (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Patients with higher isoform I showed longer overall survival.
source: Patients with higher isoform II showed significantly shorter overall survival (Figure 1F), whereas patients with higher isoform I showed longer overall survival (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Isoform II was highly expressed in OSCC tissues and positively correlated with the progression of OSCC.
source: These evidences suggested that isoform II was highly expressed in OSCC tissues and positively correlated with the progression of OSCC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The expression levels of isoform II were significantly upregulated in breast invasive carcinoma (BRCA).
source: Consistently, the expression levels of isoform II were also significantly upregulated in breast invasive carcinoma (BRCA) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), colon adenocarcinoma (COAD) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), and stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D) patients of TCGA database, suggesting that isoform II might play extensive roles in multiple cancers.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The expression levels of isoform II were significantly upregulated in colon adenocarcinoma (COAD).
source: Consistently, the expression levels of isoform II were also significantly upregulated in breast invasive carcinoma (BRCA) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), colon adenocarcinoma (COAD) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), and stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D) patients of TCGA database, suggesting that isoform II might play extensive roles in multiple cancers.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The expression levels of isoform II were significantly upregulated in prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD).
source: Consistently, the expression levels of isoform II were also significantly upregulated in breast invasive carcinoma (BRCA) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), colon adenocarcinoma (COAD) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), and stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D) patients of TCGA database, suggesting that isoform II might play extensive roles in multiple cancers.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The expression levels of isoform II were significantly upregulated in stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD).
source: Consistently, the expression levels of isoform II were also significantly upregulated in breast invasive carcinoma (BRCA) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), colon adenocarcinoma (COAD) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), and stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D) patients of TCGA database, suggesting that isoform II might play extensive roles in multiple cancers.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Isoform II might play extensive roles in multiple cancers.
source: Consistently, the expression levels of isoform II were also significantly upregulated in breast invasive carcinoma (BRCA) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), colon adenocarcinoma (COAD) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), and stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D) patients of TCGA database, suggesting that isoform II might play extensive roles in multiple cancers.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the observation that isoform II is upregulated in multiple cancer types.

claim: The ratios of isoform II vs I and the expression levels of isoform II were significantly higher in OSCC tissues than those in adjacent normal tissues.
source: As expected, the ratios of isoform II vs I and the expression levels of isoform II were also significantly higher in these OSCC tissues than those in adjacent normal tissues (Figure 1H and I).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data from clinical samples shown in Figure 1G, 1H, and 1I.

claim: RUNX2 isoform II may play important roles in OSCC.
source: These results suggested that RUNX2 isoform II may play important roles in OSCC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the expression data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Overexpression of FLAG tagged isoform II significantly promoted the proliferation of OSCC cells, CAL 27 and SCC-9 cell lines.
source: Overexpression of FLAG tagged isoform II significantly promoted the proliferation of OSCC cells, CAL 27 and SCC-9 cell lines (Figure 2A and B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 2A and B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Isoform II overexpression showed enhanced cell proliferation compared with isoform I overexpression in OSCC cells.
source: Interestingly, isoform II overexpression showed enhanced cell proliferation compared with isoform I overexpression in OSCC cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Knockdown of isoform II significantly inhibited cell proliferation in both CAL 27 and SCC-9 cell lines.
source: Consistently, knockdown of isoform II significantly inhibited cell proliferation in both cell lines (Figure 2C and D), as well as colony formation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Knockdown of isoform II significantly inhibited colony formation in both CAL 27 and SCC-9 cell lines.
source: Consistently, knockdown of isoform II significantly inhibited cell proliferation in both cell lines (Figure 2C and D), as well as colony formation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Isoform II overexpression has no effect on OSCC cell migration or invasion.
source: We found that isoform II overexpression has no effect on OSCC cell migration or invasion, while isoform I overexpression could inhibit the cell migration or invasion (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by wound healing and transwell assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Isoform I overexpression could inhibit OSCC cell migration or invasion.
source: We found that isoform II overexpression has no effect on OSCC cell migration or invasion, while isoform I overexpression could inhibit the cell migration or invasion (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by wound healing and transwell assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Cells with isoform II-knockdown showed significantly higher apoptosis than those control cells.
source: Cells with isoform II-knockdown showed significantly higher apoptosis than those control cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The overexpression of isoform II or isoform I had no obvious effect on the cellular apoptosis of OSCC.
source: However, the overexpression of isoform II or isoform I had no obvious effect on the cellular apoptosis of OSCC (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry apoptosis assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: CAL 27 cells stably transfected with shRNAs against isoform II showed significantly reduced tumor growth than those transfected with non-specific control shRNA in nude mice.
source: Importantly, CAL 27 cells stably transfected with shRNAs against isoform II showed significantly reduced tumor growth and weight than those transfected with non-specific control shRNA in nude mice (Figure 2G–J, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by nude mice xenograft data shown in Figure 2G–J and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–D.

claim: CAL 27 cells stably transfected with shRNAs against isoform II showed significantly reduced tumor weight than those transfected with non-specific control shRNA in nude mice.
source: Importantly, CAL 27 cells stably transfected with shRNAs against isoform II showed significantly reduced tumor growth and weight than those transfected with non-specific control shRNA in nude mice (Figure 2G–J, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–D).
evidence: This is supported by nude mice xenograft data shown in Figure 2G–J and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–D.

claim: RUNX2 isoform II is required for the proliferation and tumorigenicity of OSCC cells.
source: These results suggested that RUNX2 isoform II is required for the proliferation and tumorigenicity of OSCC cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Isoform II-knockdown significantly enhanced total ROS production in CAL 27 and SCC-9 cells.
source: We found that isoform II-knockdown significantly enhanced total ROS production (Figure 3A) and lipid peroxidation accumulation (Figure 3B) in CAL 27 and SCC-9 cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry ROS detection data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Isoform II-knockdown significantly enhanced lipid peroxidation accumulation in CAL 27 and SCC-9 cells.
source: We found that isoform II-knockdown significantly enhanced total ROS production (Figure 3A) and lipid peroxidation accumulation (Figure 3B) in CAL 27 and SCC-9 cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry lipid peroxidation detection data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Isoform II overexpression suppressed ROS production in CAL 27 and SCC-9 cells.
source: Consistently, isoform II overexpression suppressed ROS production (Figure 3C) and lipid peroxidation (Figure 3D) in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry ROS detection data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Isoform II overexpression suppressed lipid peroxidation in CAL 27 and SCC-9 cells.
source: Consistently, isoform II overexpression suppressed ROS production (Figure 3C) and lipid peroxidation (Figure 3D) in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry lipid peroxidation detection data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Isoform II-knockdown induced shrunken mitochondria with vanished cristae.
source: In addition, we found that isoform II-knockdown induced shrunken mitochondria with vanished cristae with transmission electron microscopy (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy images shown in Figure 3E.

claim: RUNX2 isoform II may suppress ferroptosis.
source: This phenomenon, along with the above results of ROS production and lipid peroxidation accumulation assays, suggests that RUNX2 isoform II may suppress ferroptosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data on ROS, lipid peroxidation, and mitochondrial morphology.

claim: Isoform II-knockdown cells showed more elongated mitochondria than in control cells.
source: We also found that isoform II-knockdown cells showed more elongated mitochondria than in control cells (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), which may be related to the suppression of FIS1 (Fission, Mitochondrial 1) expression by RUNX2 isoform II-knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy images and quantification shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The elongated mitochondria may be related to the suppression of FIS1 (Fission, Mitochondrial 1) expression by RUNX2 isoform II-knockdown.
source: We also found that isoform II-knockdown cells showed more elongated mitochondria than in control cells (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A), which may be related to the suppression of FIS1 (Fission, Mitochondrial 1) expression by RUNX2 isoform II-knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data showing reduced FIS1 expression upon isoform II-knockdown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The elongated mitochondria may be caused by the deficiency of mitochondrial fission.
source: And the elongated mitochondria may be caused by the deficiency of mitochondrial fission (Wang et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2024.

claim: The oxygen consumption rates (OCRs) were lower in isoform II-knockdown OSCC cells.
source: The oxygen consumption rates (OCRs) were lower in isoform II-knockdown OSCC cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse OCR assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B.

claim: Fer-1 treatment partially rescued the reduction of cell proliferation caused by isoform II-knockdown.
source: As expected, Fer-1 treatment partially rescued the reduction of cell proliferation caused by isoform II-knockdown (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data with Fer-1 treatment shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Z-VAD could partially rescue the reduction of cell proliferation caused by isoform II-knockdown.
source: We also found that Z-VAD and Nec-1 could partially rescue the reduction of cell proliferation caused by isoform II-knockdown (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 4B) and Z-VAD also could partially decrease apoptosis induced by isoform II-knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), which suggested that both apoptosis and necroptosis also contribute to the retardation of cell proliferation cause by isoform II-knockdown.
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data with Z-VAD treatment shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Nec-1 could partially rescue the reduction of cell proliferation caused by isoform II-knockdown.
source: We also found that Z-VAD and Nec-1 could partially rescue the reduction of cell proliferation caused by isoform II-knockdown (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 4B) and Z-VAD also could partially decrease apoptosis induced by isoform II-knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), which suggested that both apoptosis and necroptosis also contribute to the retardation of cell proliferation cause by isoform II-knockdown.
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data with Nec-1 treatment shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Z-VAD could partially decrease apoptosis induced by isoform II-knockdown.
source: We also found that Z-VAD and Nec-1 could partially rescue the reduction of cell proliferation caused by isoform II-knockdown (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 4B) and Z-VAD also could partially decrease apoptosis induced by isoform II-knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), which suggested that both apoptosis and necroptosis also contribute to the retardation of cell proliferation cause by isoform II-knockdown.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry apoptosis assay data with Z-VAD treatment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Both apoptosis and necroptosis contribute to the retardation of cell proliferation caused by isoform II-knockdown.
source: We also found that Z-VAD and Nec-1 could partially rescue the reduction of cell proliferation caused by isoform II-knockdown (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 4B) and Z-VAD also could partially decrease apoptosis induced by isoform II-knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 5), which suggested that both apoptosis and necroptosis also contribute to the retardation of cell proliferation cause by isoform II-knockdown.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments with Z-VAD and Nec-1.

claim: The combination of Fer-1 and Z-VAD was more effective in rescuing cell proliferation than Fer-1 or Z-VAD alone.
source: In addition, we found that the combination of Fer-1 and Z-VAD was more effective in rescuing cell proliferation than Fer-1 or Z-VAD alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by rescue efficiency analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Fer-1 treatment reduced the increased levels of ROS production caused by isoform II-knockdown.
source: Fer-1 treatment reduced the increased levels of ROS production (Figure 3H) and lipid peroxidation (Figure 3I) caused by isoform II-knockdown.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry ROS detection data with Fer-1 treatment shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Fer-1 treatment reduced the increased levels of lipid peroxidation caused by isoform II-knockdown.
source: Fer-1 treatment reduced the increased levels of ROS production (Figure 3H) and lipid peroxidation (Figure 3I) caused by isoform II-knockdown.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry lipid peroxidation detection data with Fer-1 treatment shown in Figure 3I.

claim: RSL3 could cause cell death in CAL 27 and SCC-9 cells.
source: RSL3, a ferroptosis activator, could cause cell death in CAL 27 and SCC-9 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 7A), and increase the production of cellular ROS (Figure 3—figure supplement 7B) and lipid peroxidation (Figure 3—figure supplement 7C).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data with RSL3 treatment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7A.

claim: RSL3 could increase the production of cellular ROS in CAL 27 and SCC-9 cells.
source: RSL3, a ferroptosis activator, could cause cell death in CAL 27 and SCC-9 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 7A), and increase the production of cellular ROS (Figure 3—figure supplement 7B) and lipid peroxidation (Figure 3—figure supplement 7C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry ROS detection data with RSL3 treatment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7B.

claim: RSL3 could increase lipid peroxidation in CAL 27 and SCC-9 cells.
source: RSL3, a ferroptosis activator, could cause cell death in CAL 27 and SCC-9 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 7A), and increase the production of cellular ROS (Figure 3—figure supplement 7B) and lipid peroxidation (Figure 3—figure supplement 7C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry lipid peroxidation detection data with RSL3 treatment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7C.

claim: Isoform II overexpression could elevate the IC50 values of RSL3.
source: Isoform II overexpression could elevate the IC50 values of RSL3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 8A); in contrast, isoform II-knockdown decreased the IC50 values of RSL3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 8B).
evidence: This is supported by IC50 analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8A.

claim: Isoform II-knockdown decreased the IC50 values of RSL3.
source: Isoform II overexpression could elevate the IC50 values of RSL3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 8A); in contrast, isoform II-knockdown decreased the IC50 values of RSL3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 8B).
evidence: This is supported by IC50 analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8B.

claim: Overexpression of isoform II could partially reduce the increased levels of ROS production caused by RSL3.
source: As expected, overexpression of isoform II could partially reduce the increased levels of ROS production (Figure 3J) and lipid peroxidation (Figure 3K) caused by RSL3.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry ROS detection data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Overexpression of isoform II could partially reduce the increased levels of lipid peroxidation caused by RSL3.
source: As expected, overexpression of isoform II could partially reduce the increased levels of ROS production (Figure 3J) and lipid peroxidation (Figure 3K) caused by RSL3.
